newsitem.title: USA: Developers, green groups clash on wetlands plan.
newsitem.headline: Developers, green groups clash on wetlands plan.

text.p: The Clinton administration Thursday officially announced a new wetland management policy, prompting groans from property developers and cautious applause from environmentalists.
Developers said the new plan, released by the Army Corps of Engineers, would rein in their ability to drain small wetlands areas and could increase costs for some housing and development projects.
Environmentalists, on the other hand, said the plan was a good start but could still leave too many loopholes for developers.
The Corps released its plan to phase out the Nation 26 permit programme, under which landowners could get permits to develop up to 10 acres of wetlands with minimal government review or interference.
The Nation 26 permits are used for small isolated and headwaters wetlands that the Corps previously has considered to have small environmental impact.

Michael Davis, deputy assistant secretary of the Army (Civil Works), said the Nation 26 permit was intended to screen out projects with modest impact so the Corps could devote its resources to reviewing more significant projects.
"We agree that the holes in the screen were too large," he said at a news conference, letting too many wetlands be damaged with too little review.
The lower 48 states have lost about half their wetlands -- essential for wildlife habitat, flood control and water quality -- to development.

The Corps said for the next two years, it will put tighter constraints on the permits and shrink the minimum size of wetland plots that will come under government scrutiny to three acres from 10 acres. The Corps will require that it be notified of plans to develop wetlands of at least one-third acre, down from the current one acre minimum.
After two years, the Corps is to have a new system for small wetlands which will give permit applications more individual review, and base permits on the type of proposed development.

"The effect of that will be to increase the time it takes to get a decision from the government, which will increase costs," said Michael Luzier, the National Association of Home Builders' assistant staff vice president for environmental regulations.
"I can't tell you how much it will raise houses' costs, x or y," but Luzier said the additional required lead time on projects will be factored into final costs.

"The Nationwide Permit 26 was the most destructive general permit and probably the majority of wetlands destruction authorised by the Corps has taken place under it," John Echeverria, the National Audubon Society's general counsel, said. "This is a modest step in the direction of greater balance in this programme."
But he said the plan should require more reviews by other agencies, such as the Fish and Wildlife Service, which often show more environmental concern than the Corps.
Luzier said homebuilders and other developers will appeal to Congress to halt the change, saying it will generate red tape, delays and higher costs for projects.

But Echeverria said: "Ten acres represents seven-and-a-half football fields. The idea that is always going to have minimal impacts is not defensible, and I think it's unlikely Congress will overrule the change."
